definition: A style of organising programs: what the basic building blocks are and how they are combined. Imperative, object-oriented, functional, logic and dataflow are paradigms; most languages support several.
A paradigm in which a program is a sequence of commands that change the program's state step by step. It describes how to compute a result, and mirrors how a CPU executes instructions.
example: A loop that adds each number to a running total is imperative: you spell out every step and every change to the total.

definition: A paradigm in which you describe the result you want and leave the steps to an engine, compiler or runtime. SQL, regular expressions, HTML and Kubernetes manifests are declarative.
example: SELECT SUM(x) FROM t states the result; the database decides how to scan the table.

definition: The design used by almost all computers since the 1940s: a processor that fetches instructions one after another from the same memory that holds the data, reading and writing that memory as it goes. Imperative programming mirrors it.

A low-level language whose instructions map almost one-to-one onto a processor's machine instructions, such as 'add these two registers' or 'jump to this address'. It is imperative in its purest form.
The instruction set family used by most desktop, laptop and server processors from Intel and AMD, descended from the Intel 8086 of 1978.

A tiny, very fast storage location inside the processor, holding one value (typically 64 bits on modern CPUs) that instructions work on directly. A CPU has only a few dozen. A register-based virtual machine imitates them with numbered slots in software.

All the values a running program's variables and data structures hold at a given moment. Imperative code works by changing it; mutable state shared between parts of a program is a common source of bugs.
A statement that stores a value in a variable, replacing what was there. In `x = x + 1` the `=` is a command (compute x + 1, then store it in x), not a mathematical equation.
The order in which a program's statements run, and the constructs that change it: if-statements, loops, jumps, function calls and exceptions.

Repeating a block of code, usually with a loop, either a fixed number of times or until a condition is met. With sequence and selection (if), it is one of the three structures of structured programming.
Imperative programming organised into procedures (also called functions or subroutines): named blocks of steps that can be called from elsewhere. C and Pascal are classic procedural languages.
A discipline that limits control flow to sequence, selection (if) and iteration (loops), plus subroutines, instead of arbitrary jumps. It made programs much easier to read and reason about.
A statement that jumps unconditionally to another labelled point in the program. Unrestricted use makes code hard to follow, which Dijkstra criticised in 1968.
Dutch computer scientist (1930–2002) whose 1968 letter 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful' helped launch structured programming. He also invented a well-known shortest-path algorithm.

A 1966 result by Corrado Böhm and Giuseppe Jacopini showing that any flowchart program can be rewritten using only sequence, selection and iteration, possibly with extra boolean flag variables. So goto is never strictly necessary.

A function whose result can be worked out by some step-by-step procedure (an algorithm) that always finishes, for example by a Turing machine. Every general-purpose language can express exactly these functions.
Able to compute anything a Turing machine can, given enough memory and time. All general-purpose programming languages, of every paradigm, are Turing-complete.
A diagram of a program as boxes for steps and arrows for where control goes next, including arrows that jump anywhere. Early programs were often designed this way.
A value that is either true or false. A flag variable is a boolean used to remember which state a program is in.
A language meant for writing any kind of program, such as Python, Java or Haskell, as opposed to a domain-specific language such as SQL or HTML built for one kind of task.
A language designed for one kind of problem, such as SQL for queries, HTML for documents or a configuration language for infrastructure. It trades generality for clarity in its domain.

The part of a database that turns a SQL query into an execution plan, choosing join order, indexes and parallelism from table sizes and statistics. The same SQL text can get a very different plan when indexes or statistics change.
A way for a database to join two tables: build a hash table from the smaller one, then scan the larger one and look up each row's key in it.
The order in which a database combines tables in a query with several joins. It can change the work done by orders of magnitude, so the query planner chooses it.
Finding rows by looking them up in an index (often a B-tree) instead of reading the whole table. It is fast when only a few rows match.
Reading every row of a table to find the ones that match. Fine for small tables or when most rows match, but very slow for finding a few rows in a large table.
Summary numbers a database keeps about each table, such as row counts and how values are distributed, which the query planner uses to estimate costs. Stale statistics can lead to a bad plan.
A SQL command that shows the plan the database chose for a query (scans, joins, estimated costs) instead of, or as well as, running it. It is the main tool for debugging slow queries.
An instruction embedded in a SQL query telling the planner how to run it, such as which index to use. Some databases support hints; PostgreSQL does not have them built in.

A common table expression (CTE) is a named temporary result defined with WITH at the start of a SQL query. A recursive one refers to itself, letting SQL repeat a step until no new rows appear, for example to find all ancestors.
HyperText Markup Language: the declarative language that describes the structure of web pages (headings, paragraphs, links). The browser decides how to lay it out and draw it.
Cascading Style Sheets: the declarative language that describes how web pages look, such as colours, fonts and layout rules.
A compact pattern describing a set of strings, such as `[0-9]+` for 'one or more digits'. You declare the pattern; the regex engine decides how to search for matches.
The file read by the Make build tool. It declares targets, the files they depend on and the commands that build them; Make works out which targets are out of date and rebuilds only those.

HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool. You declare the cloud resources you want in .tf files; on each plan/apply run it compares them with what exists and creates, changes or deletes resources to match.
The file in which Terraform records which real resources it manages and their last-known settings. It is refreshed from the cloud provider before each plan.
Managing servers, networks and other cloud resources through files that describe them, kept in version control, instead of clicking through a console.
An open-source system that runs containers across a cluster of machines. You declare the desired state (for example 'three copies of this web server') and its controllers keep reality matching it.
A Kubernetes program that runs in a loop, comparing the declared desired state of some resources with the observed state and acting to close the gap, for example starting a new Pod when one dies.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network address and storage and are scheduled together on one machine.
One of several identical running copies of a program, such as one Pod among three that a Kubernetes Deployment keeps running.
A Kubernetes resource that declares how many replicas of a Pod should run and which version, and rolls out changes gradually.
A file, usually YAML, that declares a Kubernetes resource and its desired state. Applying it again unchanged changes nothing.
The process of replacing running copies of an application with a new version, often a few at a time so the service stays up.
The end state you declare for a system, such as 'three replicas of version 2'. Declarative tools compare it with the actual state and act to make them match.

Comparing a declared desired state with the current state and making only the changes needed to bring them together. Kubernetes controllers do it continuously; React's reconciler does it when it compares a new UI description with the previous one.
Real infrastructure gradually differing from what was declared, for example because someone changed or deleted a resource by hand. Desired-state tools detect it on their next run.
The property that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. 'Ensure 3 replicas' is idempotent; 'start 3 containers' is not.
example: Running 'ensure 3 replicas' ten times leaves 3; running 'start 3 containers' ten times leaves 30.

definition: A JavaScript library from Meta for building user interfaces. Components describe what the UI should look like for the current state, and React works out the DOM changes needed.
A tool in React's developer tools that records which components rendered and how long each took, used to find slow parts of a UI.
A popular JavaScript library from 2006 for finding and changing elements of a web page directly, step by step: the imperative style React replaced for many apps.
Document Object Model: the browser's tree of objects representing a web page. Changing the DOM changes what is on screen.
User interface: the part of a program people see and interact with, such as screens, buttons and text.
Graphical user interface: a UI built from windows, buttons and other widgets drawn on screen, as opposed to a text command line.
Object-relational mapper: a library that lets code work with database rows as ordinary objects, writing the SQL for you. Django's ORM and Hibernate are examples.

A performance bug where code runs one query to load a list of N items, then one more query per item, N + 1 in total, often hidden behind innocent-looking attribute access in an ORM. Eager loading fixes it.
example: Loading 500 orders and then each order's customer makes 501 queries instead of 1 or 2.

definition: Fetching related data up front, for example with one join, instead of loading it later one item at a time. It avoids the N+1 problem.
Delaying a database fetch until the data is first used. Convenient, but in a loop it can fire one query per item.
One request sent to another system, such as a database, and its reply coming back. Each round trip costs at least the network and processing delay, often a millisecond or less within a data centre.
A popular Python web framework that includes an ORM. Its select_related method tells the ORM to fetch related rows with a join up front.
Doing several pieces of work at the same moment, for example on several CPU cores. Declarative code leaves engines free to add it because it does not fix an order.

Java's library (from Java 8) for processing collections as pipelines of operations such as filter, map and sum. A stream can be consumed only once, and a parallel stream can split the work across cores.
A Java stream specialised for primitive int values, avoiding the boxed Integer objects a general Stream<Integer> holds.

A compiler optimisation that merges several passes over data into one, so no intermediate list is built. Haskell's GHC does it with rewrite rules, which is safe because pure code has no order-dependent effects.

An instruction to the GHC compiler to replace one expression pattern with an equivalent faster one, such as replacing map f (map g xs) with a single map. Library authors use them to make fusion happen.
The Glasgow Haskell Compiler, the main Haskell compiler. It performs aggressive optimisations such as fusion that rely on Haskell's purity.
A spreadsheet formula, such as one using NOW or RAND, that is recalculated on every recalculation whether or not its inputs changed.
A bug where a loop runs one time too many or too few, typically from using < instead of <= or starting from 1 instead of 0.
A marker set in a debugger that pauses the program when a given line is reached, so you can inspect its state.
A tool that measures where a program spends its time or memory, so you can find what to optimise.
A feature that lets you step outside an abstraction to control the details yourself, such as a SQL hint or a React ref. Its existence shows where the abstraction leaks.
An abstraction whose hidden details still affect you, so you sometimes have to understand what is underneath it, for example a SQL query that is slow because of the plan the database chose.
A model of a system that is always in one of a fixed set of states and moves between them in response to inputs. Parsers and protocol handlers are often written this way.
A thousandth of a second (0.001 s), written ms. A database round trip within a data centre typically takes around 1 ms or less.
A thousandth of a litre, written ml or mL. A teaspoon holds about 5 ml.

Object-oriented programming: a paradigm that organises a program around objects, bundles of data (fields) and the operations (methods) allowed on it. Encapsulation, inheritance, composition and polymorphism are its main ideas.
A function that belongs to an object or class and is called on an object, as in `account.deposit(100)`. Inside it, the object is available as `self` (Python) or `this` (Java, JavaScript).

The object or process a call or message is sent to. In OOP it is the object a method is called on, `obj` in `obj.m(arg)`, and in single dispatch only the receiver's runtime class decides which method body runs. In message-passing concurrency it is the process that takes the message.
A language from the Norwegian Computing Center (1967), built for simulations, that introduced classes, objects, inheritance and virtual methods: the first object-oriented language.
An object-oriented language developed by Alan Kay and colleagues at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, in which everything, even a number, is an object and all computation is objects sending messages.
American computer scientist who led the Smalltalk work at Xerox PARC and is generally credited with coining the term 'object-oriented'. He has said the key idea was messaging between objects.
Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center in California, where in the 1970s researchers created Smalltalk, the graphical user interface and Ethernet, among much else.
Objects (or processes) communicating only by sending each other requests, with each receiver deciding how to respond. In Smalltalk, calling a method is described as sending a message.
Hiding an object's internal data and allowing changes only through its methods, so the object can keep its invariants (rules that must always hold, such as 'balance is never negative').
A class reusing and extending another class: the subclass gets the parent's fields and methods and may override some. It also makes the subclass a subtype, usable wherever the parent is expected.
A class inheriting from more than one parent class, as Python and C++ allow and Java does not. It raises the question of which parent's method wins, answered in Python by the MRO.
A class that inherits from another class (its superclass or parent) and may add to or override what it inherits.
The class another class inherits from, also called its parent or base class.
A subclass providing its own version of a method it inherited, with the same signature. Which version runs is decided at run time by the object's actual class.
Defining several methods or functions with the same name but different parameter types, such as print(int) and print(String). In Java the compiler picks one from the declared argument types.
A type whose values can be used wherever values of another type (its supertype) are expected. A Dog class that extends Animal is a subtype of Animal.
Using existing code again instead of rewriting it. Inheritance gives it by copying a parent's implementation into a subclass; composition gives it by calling another object.
Subclasses breaking when their parent class changes internally, because they depended on how the parent works rather than only on what it promises.
example: A counting subclass of HashSet counts 6 instead of 3 because the parent's addAll quietly calls add.

definition: A widely read book of Java best practices by Joshua Bloch, a designer of the Java collections library (third edition 2018). It warns about the risks of inheritance.
American software engineer who led the design of the Java collections framework and wrote Effective Java.
Java's standard set class backed by a hash table: it stores each distinct element once and checks membership in roughly constant time.
Java's sorted set class, backed by a red-black tree. It needs its elements to have an ordering, so it behaves differently from HashSet for nulls and equality.
A Java class that provides default implementations of collection methods in terms of a few others; its addAll simply calls add once per element.
Java's standard growable array list class.
Java's old stack class. It extends the list-like Vector class, so it exposes methods such as insertElementAt that break last-in-first-out behaviour: a well-known misuse of inheritance.
Last in, first out: the rule of a stack, where the most recently added item is the first removed.
The rule that a subtype must be usable anywhere its parent type is, without surprising callers: it must keep the parent's promises. Introduced by Barbara Liskov in 1987.
example: A mutable Square that is a subclass of Rectangle breaks it: setting width 5 then height 2 gives area 4, not 10.

definition: American computer scientist (born 1939) who designed the CLU language and formulated the Liskov substitution principle. She received the Turing Award in 2008.
The design rule that code should be open for extension but closed for modification: you add behaviour by adding new code rather than editing existing code.
What a class or function promises callers: what inputs it accepts, what it returns and what rules it keeps. Code should depend only on the contract, not on how it is implemented.
Building an object out of other objects that it holds and calls (a has-a relationship), instead of inheriting from them. It couples classes only through public behaviour.
Handing a request on to another object or function rather than doing the work yourself. In OOP, an object delegates to a helper object it holds instead of inheriting the behaviour.
A design pattern in which a wrapper object implements the same interface as the object it wraps, forwards calls to it, and adds behaviour such as counting or logging.

The 1994 book by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides (the 'Gang of Four') that catalogued 23 reusable object-oriented designs, such as visitor and decorator, and advised favouring composition over inheritance.
A relationship where one type is a kind of another, like a Dog is an Animal. It is the only good reason for inheritance.
A relationship where one object contains another as a part, like a Car has an Engine. Modelled with composition.
A relationship where one object calls another without owning it or being a kind of it, like a service using a logger. Modelled by passing the helper in.
A record type grouping named fields together, as in C, Go and Rust. Go's struct embedding lets one struct include another and automatically forward its methods.
In Rust (and Scala), a named set of methods that types can implement, used for polymorphism instead of class inheritance. Similar to an interface in Java.
A Rust block, written `impl Type { ... }`, that defines the methods of a struct or enum, or implements a trait for it.
Code written for a parent type working on any of its subtypes, each supplying its own behaviour. This is what OOP usually means by polymorphism.
One name having separate implementations for different types, chosen by type, as with overloading print(int) and print(String) or Haskell type classes.
Code written once with a type parameter that works identically for any type, such as List<T> in Java. Usually called generics.
Accepting any object that has the methods you call, whatever its declared type or class: 'if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck'. Python and JavaScript work this way.

Choosing which piece of code runs for an operation. For a call, it is how a language picks which function or method body runs, either at compile time (static) or at run time (dynamic); in an interpreter, the dispatch loop picks the handler for each instruction.
Choosing which method body to run at run time from the actual class of the object, so an inherited method calling speak() runs the subclass's version.
Choosing which function body to run at compile time from declared types, so the call can be a direct jump or be inlined.
Dispatch in which only the receiver's runtime type chooses the method; argument types are fixed at compile time. Java, C# and Python method calls work this way.
Choosing an operation from the runtime types of two objects. Single-dispatch languages fake it with two virtual calls, as in the visitor pattern.
Choosing which function body runs from the runtime types of all its arguments, not just the first. Used by Common Lisp's CLOS and Julia.
example: collide(asteroid, ship) and collide(ship, ship) can have separate bodies chosen at run time.

definition: A per-class table of pointers to method bodies, commonly used to implement dynamic dispatch: each object points to its class's table, and a call looks the method up by position.
The hidden pointer inside an object that points to its class's virtual method table.
Application binary interface: the low-level rules compiled code follows, such as how objects are laid out in memory and how functions are called, so separately compiled pieces work together.
A compiler optimisation that replaces a function call with a copy of the function's body, removing the call's overhead and enabling further optimisations.
A place in the code where a function or method is called. A monomorphic call site has only ever seen one receiver class, which lets a JIT compiler inline the target.
The record a JIT compiler such as HotSpot keeps of which classes have actually appeared at a call site, used to decide whether inlining is worthwhile.
The main Java virtual machine implementation, from Oracle and OpenJDK. It profiles running code and JIT-compiles hot methods, inlining calls where profiles show it is safe.
Java Virtual Machine: the program that runs Java bytecode, also used by Kotlin, Scala and Clojure. It does not eliminate tail calls.
Java Development Kit: the Java compiler, standard library and tools needed to build Java programs.
The Java compiler, which turns .java source into JVM bytecode. It emits instructions such as invokevirtual; the JVM picks the target at run time.
JVM bytecode instructions for calling an instance method (invokevirtual) or an interface method (invokeinterface). The JVM chooses the actual method from the receiver's class at run time.
When source code is being translated by a compiler, before the program runs. Decisions made then cost nothing at run time and errors found then never reach users.
When the program is actually executing, as opposed to when it is being compiled.
The software that supports a running program, such as the JVM, a JavaScript engine or Python's interpreter, handling memory, dispatch and so on.
The type a variable or expression has in the source code, known to the compiler. A variable declared as Object has static type Object even if it holds a String at run time.
The actual class of the object a value refers to while the program runs, which may be a subtype of its static type.
A standardised dialect of Lisp (ANSI, 1994) with a powerful object system, CLOS, and special variables for opt-in dynamic scope.
The Common Lisp Object System, which uses generic functions with multiple dispatch: the method chosen depends on the runtime types of all arguments.
A language for numerical and scientific computing (first released 2012) built around multiple dispatch.

A design pattern in which each operation over a fixed set of node classes is a separate visitor class with one visit method per node type. New operations are cheap; new node types mean changing every visitor.
Method resolution order: the list of classes Python searches, in order, to find an attribute or method. With multiple inheritance it is computed by C3 linearisation; super() follows it.
example: For class D(B, C) where B and C inherit from A, the MRO is D, B, C, A, object.

definition: The algorithm Python (and others) use to order a class's ancestors for the MRO. It keeps each class before its parents, keeps parents in the order listed, and puts each class in the list exactly once.
In Python, a call that finds the next class after the current one in the instance's MRO, which in multiple inheritance is not always the direct parent. In Java, super refers to the parent class.

A Python object that controls attribute access by defining __get__ (and possibly __set__ or __delete__). Functions are non-data descriptors, which is how they become bound methods; properties are data descriptors.

Object-oriented programming without classes as the basic unit: each object links to another object, its prototype, and property lookups that miss walk along that chain. JavaScript works this way, with class syntax layered on top.
Syntax that makes something easier to write without adding a new capability: it could be rewritten in more basic constructs. JavaScript's class keyword is largely sugar over prototypes.

Python's renaming of attributes written with two leading underscores inside a class: self.__balance in class Account becomes _Account__balance. It avoids clashes in subclasses but is not real privacy.

A Python name that starts and ends with double underscores, such as __init__ or __len__ ('dunder' is short for 'double underscore'). Python calls these special methods itself and does not mangle them.
A single class that knows and does far too much, so most of the program depends on it. It defeats encapsulation.
Methods that only read (get) or write (set) one field. Providing them for every field exposes the internals and leaves no invariants to protect.

A paradigm that builds programs by combining functions in the mathematical sense, which return the same output for the same input and have no side effects, instead of sequencing commands that change state.

A function whose result depends only on its arguments and which has no side effects: no changing outside variables, no I/O, no reading the clock. Calling it twice with the same arguments always gives the same answer.
example: add(2, 3) is pure; a function that reads time.time() is not.

definition: A function that has side effects or depends on hidden inputs such as global variables, the clock or a database, so it may give different results for the same arguments.
Anything a function does besides returning a value that other code can observe: changing a variable outside itself, writing a file, printing, sending a network request.
The property that an expression can be replaced by its value without changing what the program does. Calls to pure functions on immutable values have it.
example: If add(2, 3) is referentially transparent, every add(2, 3) in the program can be replaced by 5.

definition: A tiny mathematical model of computation devised by Alonzo Church in the 1930s, containing nothing but function definition and function application. It is as powerful as a Turing machine and underlies functional programming.
American mathematician and logician (1903–1995) who invented the lambda calculus.
A family of languages begun by John McCarthy in 1958, built around lists and functions, in which programs are themselves lists. Scheme, Common Lisp, Clojure and Emacs Lisp are members.

Meta Language: a functional language family from the 1970s (Robin Milner) with type inference, algebraic data types and pattern matching. OCaml, Standard ML and F# descend from it; it strongly influenced Rust, Scala and Swift.
A purely functional, lazily evaluated language first defined in 1990, named after Haskell Curry. Side effects are tracked in types such as IO.
A functional language from Ericsson (1986) for highly concurrent, fault-tolerant systems such as telephone switches, built on lightweight processes that communicate by messages.
A functional language (2012) that runs on Erlang's virtual machine, with a friendlier syntax, used for concurrent web services.
A language on the JVM (2004) that combines object-oriented and functional programming.
A Lisp dialect on the JVM (2007) built around immutable persistent data structures.
Microsoft's functional-first language for .NET (2005), descended from ML/OCaml, with objects available when needed.
A functional-first language in the ML family (1996) with objects and mutable state available, popular for compilers and tools.
A function written inline without a name, such as `lambda n: n * n` in Python or `n => n * n` in JavaScript. Named after the lambda calculus.
Python syntax that builds a list from another sequence by stating what each element is and which to keep, such as [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]. It is more declarative than a loop.
Data that is never changed after it is created; to 'change' it you make a new value. It removes bugs caused by code changing shared data behind your back.
Changing a value in place, for example appending to a list, so that every reference to it sees the change.
Changing the existing object rather than building a new one, as Python's list.sort() and JavaScript's arr.sort() do.
Only the top level of an object is protected from change; objects it refers to, such as a nested list, can still be mutated. JavaScript's Object.freeze and Python's frozen dataclasses are shallow.
Every object reachable from a value is immutable, all the way down, not just the top level.
A JavaScript function that makes an object's own properties read-only. Writes are silently ignored (or throw in strict mode). It is shallow: nested objects stay changeable.
A JavaScript (and other languages') declaration that stops a name from being rebound. It does not make the value immutable: a const array can still be pushed to.
A fixed-length, ordered group of values; in Python an immutable sequence such as (1, 2). Its contents may still be mutable objects.
Python's immutable set type. Once created, elements cannot be added or removed.
A Java class (final from Java 16) that is a plain data carrier: its fields are final and its equals, hashCode and toString are generated. It is shallowly immutable.
A Java method that creates an unmodifiable list. Elements cannot be added or removed, but the elements themselves may be mutable objects.
Haskell's type for actions that interact with the outside world, such as reading files. A function returning IO is marked as effectful in its type, keeping ordinary functions pure.
A Haskell type for computations that use mutable variables and arrays internally but are pure from the outside, because the mutation cannot escape.
In functional programming, a pattern for chaining computations that carry extra context, such as possible failure, state or I/O. Haskell uses monads such as IO to keep effects explicit.
A data structure that keeps its old versions when 'changed': each update returns a new version that shares most of its memory with the old one, so updates are cheap and nothing is mutated.
Reusing the unchanged parts of an old data structure inside a new version, so only the changed path has to be copied.

The power you raise a base to in order to get a number: log base 2 of 1,024 is 10, because 2 multiplied by itself 10 times is 1,024. It grows very slowly, so logarithmic costs stay small for huge inputs.
Cost that grows with the square of the input size n. Doubling n makes the work about four times larger.
Cost that grows in direct proportion to the input size n. Doubling n doubles the work.
A function that is an ordinary value: it can be stored in a variable, passed as an argument and returned from another function.
A function that takes another function as an argument or returns one, such as map (apply a function to every element), filter (keep elements a function approves) and reduce.

A function that walks a list combining each element with an accumulator to produce one value. Sum, maximum and length are all folds; Python calls it reduce. (Compilers use 'fold' differently: constant folding works out a constant expression at compile time.)
Haskell's left fold: it combines from the left, so foldl f z [a, b, c] is f (f (f z a) b) c. foldl' is the strict version that avoids building thunks.
Haskell's right fold: it combines from the right, so foldr f z [a, b, c] is f a (f b (f c z)).
Python's left fold: reduce(f, xs, seed) combines the seed with each element of xs in turn using f.
A variable that collects a running result, such as a running total updated on each step of a loop or fold.

The property that the grouping of brackets does not change a result: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). Subtraction is not associative, and floating-point addition is not exactly associative because of rounding. In a grammar, an operator's associativity is the rule for grouping a chain of it: left-associative 10 − 4 − 3 means (10 − 4) − 3.
A value that leaves others unchanged when combined with them, such as 0 for addition or 1 for multiplication.
The usual way computers store real numbers: a fixed number of significant digits plus an exponent. Results are rounded, so (a + b) + c can differ slightly from a + (b + c).

Checking a value against a series of shapes and pulling out its parts in one step, such as 'an empty list' or 'a Circle with radius r'. Found in Haskell, Rust, Scala, Python's match (3.10) and Java 21's switch.
The input for which a recursive function answers directly without recursing, such as the empty list. Every recursion needs one to stop.
The first element of a list (the head) and the list of all remaining elements (the tail). Haskell writes the pattern as (x:xs); Prolog as [H|T].
The block of memory on the call stack holding one active function call's local variables and return address. It is created when the function is called and removed when it returns.
The region of memory recording the chain of active function calls, one stack frame per call, newest on top. It has a limited size.
Running out of call-stack space, usually from recursion that is too deep or never ends. The program crashes or raises an error.
A call that is the very last thing a function does, so nothing is left to do after it returns. In return 1 + f(x) the call to f is not a tail call, because the addition comes after.
Reusing the current stack frame for a tail call instead of adding a new one, so deep tail recursion runs in constant stack space. CPython, V8 and the JVM do not do it.
The ECMAScript 2015 requirement that tail calls in strict-mode JavaScript not grow the stack. Safari's JavaScriptCore implements it; V8 (Chrome, Node.js) and others do not.
An annotation in Scala (@tailrec) and modifier in Kotlin (tailrec) that asks the compiler to turn a self-recursive tail call into a loop, and reports an error if it cannot.
The maximum depth of nested Python calls before CPython raises RecursionError, 1,000 by default. It protects the underlying C stack from overflowing.
The Python exception raised when calls nest deeper than the recursion limit (1,000 by default).
A crash caused by a program accessing memory it is not allowed to, such as overflowing the C stack.
Turning a function of several arguments into a chain of one-argument functions, each returning the next. Named after Haskell Curry; every Haskell function works this way.
example: add x y = x + y is curried: add 10 is a function waiting for y.

definition: American logician (1900–1982) after whom currying and the Haskell language are named.
Supplying only some of a function's arguments to get a new function that takes the rest. Python's functools.partial does it explicitly.
Joining two functions so the output of one becomes the input of the other: f composed with g, written f ∘ g in maths or f . g in Haskell, means 'apply g, then f'.
Defining a function only by composing other functions, without naming its argument, as in shout = map toUpper . reverse.
An object that hands out the elements of a sequence one at a time on request. In Python 3, map and filter return lazy iterators that can be consumed only once.
The Python exception an iterator raises internally to say it has no more items. Loops and sum handle it themselves.
A Java exception meaning a method was called at the wrong time, for example reusing a stream that has already been consumed.
An exception (in Python and JavaScript) raised when an operation gets a value of the wrong type, such as reduce on an empty array with no initial value in JavaScript.
The Python exception for an argument of the right type but an unacceptable value, such as a negative deposit amount.

A Python decorator that memoises a function: it stores each result in a dictionary keyed by the arguments, which must be hashable, and returns the stored result on repeat calls. It never expires entries.
Caching a function's results by its arguments so a repeated call returns the stored answer instead of recomputing. It is only correct if the function is pure: the arguments must capture every input.
The value used to look up a cached result. For memoisation it is the function's arguments, so any hidden input left out of it can make results stale.

In Python, an object that has a fixed hash value and can be compared for equality, so it can be a dictionary key or set element. Immutable built-ins like int, str and tuple (of hashable items) are hashable; lists are not.
Several tasks being in progress at overlapping times, such as threads handling requests. When they share mutable data they can interfere with each other.

A design, named by Gary Bernhardt, that keeps the program's decisions in pure functions (the core) and puts all side effects, such as database, network and clock access, in a thin outer layer (the shell) that calls them.
Programmer and screencaster (Destroy All Software) who named the 'functional core, imperative shell' pattern in a 2012 screencast.
The part of a program that encodes the real-world rules it exists for, such as how tax or discounts are calculated, as opposed to plumbing like databases and networking.
A fake stand-in for a real dependency, such as a database or clock, used in tests. Pure functions need none, because all their inputs are arguments.
Input/output: a program communicating with the outside world, such as reading files, printing or using the network. It is a side effect.
The 2023 edition of the JavaScript standard, which added non-mutating array methods such as toSorted.
The 2015 edition of the JavaScript standard (also called ES6), a major update that added class syntax, let and const, arrow functions, modules and proper tail calls.
The 2009 edition of the JavaScript standard, which added array methods such as map, filter and reduce, and strict mode.
The official standard that defines the JavaScript language, published by Ecma International (as ECMA-262), with a new edition each year since 2015.
The programming language of web browsers (1995), also run on servers through Node.js. It is multi-paradigm: imperative, functional and prototype-based object-oriented.
An opt-in JavaScript mode (enabled with 'use strict', and always on in ES modules and classes) that turns some silent mistakes into errors, such as writing to a frozen object's property.
JavaScript's standard module system (import and export), introduced in ES2015. Module code always runs in strict mode.
Google's JavaScript engine, used by Chrome and Node.js. It does not implement proper tail calls.
The JavaScript engine of Apple's WebKit, used by Safari. It is the major engine that implements ES2015 proper tail calls.
The browser engine behind Safari, developed mainly by Apple, which includes the JavaScriptCore JavaScript engine.
A runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser, on servers, using Google's V8 engine.
Having memory reclaimed automatically by a garbage collector once no live reference can reach it. An object that is still reachable, for example from a closure, is not collected.
A paradigm in which a program is a set of facts and rules written in a form of logic, and you run it by asking a query; the system searches for values that make the query true.
The classic logic programming language, created by Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel in Marseille in 1972. It answers queries by unification and depth-first search with backtracking.
A widely used free implementation of Prolog, with libraries such as CLP(FD) for constraint solving.
A statement a logic program takes as simply true, such as parent(tom, bob). Facts are the program's data.
A statement that something is true if some other things are, written head :- body, such as ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y). The head is the part before :-.
A question put to a database or logic program. In SQL it asks for rows; in Prolog, ?- ancestor(tom, Who) asks for every Who that makes the statement true.

One self-contained part of a larger construct, such as a for clause in a comprehension or a WHERE clause in SQL. In Prolog, a clause is one fact or one rule; Prolog tries the clauses for a predicate from top to bottom, so their order affects the order of answers and even whether the search terminates.

A function or relation that is true or false for its arguments, such as the test passed to filter. In logic programming, a predicate is a named relation such as parent or append, defined by facts and rules; append/3 means the predicate append with 3 arguments.
The order in which Prolog tries the conditions (goals) in a rule's body: left to right. Like clause order, it changes the search and can decide whether it terminates.
The number of arguments a function or predicate takes: append/3 has arity 3. A term's functor is its name, such as f in f(X, b).
A Prolog term built from a name and arguments, such as f(a, X) or cons(1, nil). Compound terms let Prolog build nested data like lists and trees; basic Datalog forbids them.

Finding values for variables that make two terms identical, if any exist. Prolog uses it to match queries against facts and rule heads, in both directions, so inputs and outputs are not fixed; type checkers use the same idea to infer types.
example: f(X, b) and f(a, Y) unify with X = a and Y = b; f(X, X) and f(a, b) do not.

definition: A search method that tries one choice at a time and, when a path fails, goes back to the most recent choice and tries the next alternative.
The formal name for Prolog's proof procedure: Selective Linear Definite clause resolution. In practice it is depth-first search with backtracking over the clauses.
A rule whose first goal calls the same rule again, such as ancestor(X, Y) :- ancestor(X, Z), .... In Prolog's depth-first search it calls itself forever without reaching a fact.
A Prolog feature that remembers the answers to calls already in progress, so left-recursive or cyclic programs terminate where plain Prolog would loop.
Treating anything that cannot be proved from the known facts as false. Databases and Prolog both make it: no matching row or fact means 'no'.
Prolog's 'not', written \+ G: it succeeds if the goal G cannot be proved (finitely fails) from the program, which is weaker than proving G false in classical logic.
Negation in ordinary logic: 'not P' is true only when P is actually false, not merely unproven.
A restricted logic language with no compound terms. Basic positive Datalog over finitely many constants always terminates, so it is used for database queries and code analysis.
The state where applying the rules again adds nothing new. Bottom-up Datalog evaluation stops there.
Evaluating rules by repeatedly applying all of them to the known facts to derive new facts, until nothing new appears. Unlike Prolog's top-down search it is unaffected by rule order.
An optimisation of bottom-up evaluation in which each round only combines facts that were new in the previous round, avoiding re-deriving old facts.
In logic programming, the name of a compound term, such as cons in cons(1, nil). Function-free Datalog has none, so only finitely many facts can exist.
All the pairs connected by a chain of steps in a relation, such as every ancestor reached by following parent links.
GitHub's code analysis engine and its Datalog-descended query language, used to find security bugs by querying a database built from source code.
A fast Datalog engine used for static program analysis, for example by the Doop analyser for Java.
A framework of Datalog rules for analysing Java programs, such as working out what objects each variable may point to.
A database by Cognitect that stores immutable facts over time and is queried with a dialect of Datalog.
An open-source policy engine that decides questions like 'may this user do this?' from rules written in Rego.
The policy language of Open Policy Agent, inspired by Datalog.
A service that evaluates rules about who may do what, separate from the application code that asks.
Logic programming extended with constraints over domains such as integers, so you state the conditions a solution must meet and a solver finds values. CLP(FD) means constraints over finite domains.
The part of a compiler that checks every expression is used consistently with its type, rejecting programs that would, say, add a number to a function.
The part of the Rust compiler that works out which trait implementations apply to which types, a search much like logic programming.

Haskell's mechanism for ad hoc polymorphism: a named set of operations (such as Num with + and *) that types can implement. The compiler resolves which implementation to use by a logic-programming-style search.
Examining source code for bugs or properties without running it, for example finding where untrusted input can reach a SQL query.
Following untrusted data from where it enters a program (such as a web form) to where it could do harm (such as a SQL query).
Working out which objects each variable or pointer in a program may refer to. Datalog engines such as Soufflé do it for large Java programs.

A paradigm in which a program is a directed graph: nodes are operations, edges carry values, and a node runs when its inputs are ready. Order comes only from data dependencies, so independent nodes can run in parallel.
A set of nodes joined by one-way arrows (edges). If no path leads back to where it started it is acyclic (a DAG).
Having no cycles: you can never follow the arrows of a graph back to where you started. A cyclic dependency graph has no valid evaluation order.
The CPU register holding the address of the next instruction to run. Imperative programs step it through statements; dataflow programs have no single one.
One computation needing the result of another before it can run. In dataflow and spreadsheets these dependencies alone decide the order.
A directed graph showing which items depend on which, such as spreadsheet cells, build targets or reactive values. Updating in topological order of it gives correct results.
An ordering of a directed acyclic graph's nodes in which every node comes after everything it depends on. Recalculating in this order never reads a stale value.
example: If C1 uses B1 and B1 uses A1, the topological order is A1, B1, C1.

definition: A spreadsheet formula that depends on its own cell, directly or through others, making the dependency graph cyclic. Excel reports it as an error unless iterative calculation is turned on.
An Excel option that recalculates a circular model repeatedly until values change by less than a set amount or a maximum number of iterations is reached.
Microsoft's spreadsheet program. Formula cells form a dependency graph and are recalculated in dependency order when inputs change.
Python's standard module for graph operations. Its TopologicalSorter yields nodes in topological order and raises CycleError if the graph has a cycle.
The | operator in a Unix shell, which feeds one program's output straight into the next program's input, so the programs form a chain and can run at the same time.
example: cat log | grep ERROR | sort finds error lines and sorts them.

definition: A tool that turns source files into programs by running compilers and other steps, rebuilding only what depends on files that changed. Make and Bazel are examples.
Google's open-source build system, which tracks dependencies precisely so it can rebuild and test only what changed.
National Instruments' visual programming environment for lab instruments and test equipment, programmed by wiring blocks together in a dataflow diagram.
MathWorks' graphical environment for modelling and simulating control systems as connected blocks, often generating code from the model.
A language in which programs are built by arranging and connecting graphical blocks instead of writing text.
A form of dataflow where every node runs in step with a global clock tick and uses a fixed amount of data each time, so timing and memory can be worked out before the program runs.
An industrial toolset descended from the Lustre synchronous dataflow language, used to build certified safety-critical software for aircraft, trains and power plants.
Software whose failure could injure or kill people, such as flight controls, which must meet strict certification standards.
The electronic systems on aircraft, such as flight control and navigation.
A programming model and set of libraries for defining batch and streaming data pipelines as dataflow graphs, which then run on engines such as Flink or Spark.
An open-source engine for processing data streams and batches across a cluster as dataflow graphs.
An open-source engine for large-scale data processing that builds a graph of transformations and runs it across a cluster.
Google's machine-learning library. Version 1.x had you build a computation graph first and then run it in a session; version 2 runs operations immediately by default.
Programming with values that update automatically when the values they depend on change, as spreadsheet cells do. Used in UI frameworks to keep the screen in step with state.
A value holder in a reactive UI library that records which computations read it and notifies them when it changes. Computed signals derive their value from other signals.
A JavaScript UI library built on fine-grained reactive signals that update only the affected parts of the page.
The reactive signals library from the Preact project (a small React alternative), with signal() and computed() values.
Google's TypeScript web framework, which added reactive signals in version 16 (2023), first as a developer preview.
A JavaScript UI framework whose ref() values are reactive: reading one in a computed value or template records a dependency.
In reactive programming, a moment when a derived value is computed from a mix of new and stale inputs, giving a state the formulas never allow. Updating in topological order prevents it.
Updating dependants immediately whenever a source value changes, as opposed to recomputing values lazily when they are read (pull-based).
Something registered to be notified when a value changes, such as a computed value that depends on it.
An association between a name and what it stands for: a value, a memory location, a type or a function. Languages differ in when bindings are fixed, from language design time to run time.
Making an existing name refer to a different value or object. Rebinding a local name inside a function does not affect the caller's variable, unlike mutating the object both names refer to.
When a binding is fixed: at language design, compile time, link or load time, or run time. Earlier binding usually means faster code; later binding means more flexibility.
Fixing what a name refers to before the program runs, usually at compile time.
Looking up what a name refers to only when it is used at run time. Python closures do this, so a closure created in a loop sees the loop variable's final value.
The tool that combines compiled pieces of a program and resolves calls between them, for example fixing a call to printf to the address of the library function.
A fixed position inside a function's stack frame where a compiler keeps one local variable.

The region of program text in which a name refers to a particular binding. Outside it, the same name may refer to something else or to nothing. More loosely, a 'scoped' resource or task lasts only until the block that created it ends.

How long a variable or object actually exists while the program runs. It can differ from scope: a C static local is visible only in its block but lives for the whole program. Rust checks at compile time that no reference outlives its value's lifetime.
A C variable declared static inside a function: visible only in that block, but created once and kept for the whole run of the program.
Scope limited to the block (usually a pair of braces) where a name is declared. JavaScript's let and const are block-scoped; Python has no block scope.
Scope covering a whole function, wherever in it the name is declared. JavaScript's var and Python's local variables are function-scoped.
Scoping in which a name refers to the binding in the nearest enclosing block of the source text, so you can work it out by reading the code. Almost every modern language uses it.
Scoping in which a name refers to the most recent binding on the call stack at run time, so a function's behaviour depends on who called it. Bash and early Lisps work this way.
A Common Lisp variable declared to be dynamically scoped, so a temporary rebinding is seen by every function called while it is in effect.
Python's module for context variables, values that are set for the current task or thread of execution and seen by the code it calls: an explicit, opt-in form of dynamic scope.
A React feature that passes a value down to every component beneath a provider without threading it through each component's parameters.
Python's name lookup order: Local, Enclosing function, Global (module) and Built-in. Class bodies are not part of it.
A variable that belongs to one call of a function and exists only inside it. In Python, assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local throughout that function.
A variable defined at the top level of a module or program, visible to code throughout it.
A name Python provides everywhere without importing it, such as len, print or sum. Built-ins are searched last in LEGB.
A Python declaration that makes assignments to a name inside a nested function rebind the variable in the nearest enclosing function, instead of creating a new local.
A Python declaration, written global x, that makes assignments to x inside a function rebind the module-level variable.
The Python exception raised when a function reads a local variable before assigning it, often because a later assignment made the name local for the whole function.
The Python exception raised when a name is not found in any scope (local, enclosing, global or built-in).

A keyword for declaring a variable. In JavaScript, var is the original declaration: it is function-scoped, so a loop using var shares one variable across all iterations, and modern style uses let or const instead. In Java (from Java 10) and C#, var instead declares a local variable whose type the compiler infers.
JavaScript's block-scoped variable declaration from ES2015. A for loop declared with let gets a fresh binding on every iteration.
In language implementation, the set of variable bindings available to a piece of code. A closure carries the environment it was created in.

A variable from an enclosing scope that a closure uses. Languages either share the variable itself with the closure (Python, JavaScript) or let you choose to copy it (by value) or refer to it (by reference), as C++ and Rust do.
A value a parameter takes when the caller does not supply one. Python evaluates it once, when the def statement runs.
A Python bug pattern: a default such as acc=[] is created once and shared by every call, so changes made in one call appear in the next. Use None and create the list inside the function.
The problem of a function returning an inner function that uses its local variables: those variables must outlive the stack frame, so they have to be stored somewhere longer-lived, usually the heap.

The region of memory for data that must outlive the function that created it. It is managed by a garbage collector or by explicit freeing, and is slower to allocate than the stack. It has nothing to do with the heap data structure.
The small CPython object that holds a variable captured by a closure. The outer function and every closure over that variable share the same cell, so changes made with nonlocal are seen by all.
Lua's name for a captured variable. It points into the stack while the outer function runs and is moved ('closed') to the heap when that function returns.
In C, a value holding the address of a function so it can be called indirectly. It carries no environment, so C callbacks take a separate void * context argument.
A function passed to other code to be called later, for example when a timer fires or a button is clicked.
A callback registered to run when something happens, such as a click. If it is a closure, it keeps everything it captured alive while it remains registered.
In C and C++, an operation the language standard places no requirements on, such as using a reference to a destroyed variable. The program may crash, give wrong answers or appear to work.
A reference or pointer to memory whose object no longer exists. Using it is undefined behaviour in C++; safe Rust rejects it at compile time.

Rust's compile-time rules that every value has one owner and that borrowed references cannot outlive the value they refer to. They rule out dangling references and data races without a garbage collector.
A Rust closure marked move, which takes its captured values by value (moving or copying them in) instead of borrowing them.
An object is reachable if a running program can still get to it by following references from its variables. Garbage collectors free only unreachable objects.
The rules for when a function's argument expressions are evaluated and what the function receives: for example call by value, call by reference, call by sharing, call by name and call by need.
Evaluating every argument to a value before the function is called. Most languages are strict.
Evaluating an argument only if and when the function actually uses it. Call by name and call by need are non-strict.
Passing a copy of the argument's value to a function, so assigning to the parameter cannot affect the caller. Java passes everything this way, including copies of object references.
Passing the caller's variable itself, so the parameter is an alias for it and assigning to the parameter changes the caller's variable, as with C++ int& or C# ref.

Passing a copy of a reference to the argument's object. Mutating the object is visible to the caller; assigning a new object to the parameter is not. Python, JavaScript and Ruby objects behave this way.
Passing an argument unevaluated and evaluating it again every time the parameter is used. It was Algol 60's default and is available for Scala's => parameters.
Call by name with caching: an argument is evaluated the first time it is used and the result is reused afterwards. It is how Haskell's lazy evaluation works.
Delaying a computation until its result is actually needed, and then doing it at most once. Haskell evaluates everything this way; Python generators and iterators are lazy too.
A suspended computation stored in place of a value until it is needed. Long chains of thunks can use a lot of memory.
A marker in Haskell code that forces a value to be evaluated now rather than left as a thunk, used to stop memory building up.
A Python function containing yield, which produces values lazily one at a time as they are requested, instead of building a whole list.
Evaluating the second operand of and/or only if the first does not already decide the result, as in x is not None and x.ok.
An expression that picks one of two values based on a condition: a if c else b in Python, c ? a : b in JavaScript. Only the chosen branch is evaluated.
An Algol 60 trick that uses call by name to pass an expression and a loop variable together, so a single sum procedure can add up any formula.
Two names referring to the same memory or object, so a change through one is seen through the other. Compilers must prove there is no aliasing before reordering some operations.
A name in a function definition that stands for a value the caller supplies; the supplied value is the argument.
Python's augmented assignment. For a list it calls __iadd__, which extends the same list in place; for immutable types such as int or tuple it computes a new value and rebinds the name.
A Python dataclass declared with frozen=True, whose fields cannot be reassigned after creation (doing so raises FrozenInstanceError). It is shallow: a list stored in a field can still be mutated.
The exception Python raises when code tries to assign to a field of a frozen dataclass.
A language that supports several paradigms, such as Python, Scala or Rust, which mix imperative, object-oriented and functional styles.
A popular general-purpose language (1991) by Guido van Rossum, mainly imperative and object-oriented with functional features such as lambdas and comprehensions.
The standard implementation of Python, written in C. It has no tail-call optimisation and a default recursion limit of 1,000.
Dutch programmer who created Python and led it until 2018. He deliberately rejected tail-call optimisation, partly to keep full tracebacks.
The list of nested function calls active when an error happened, printed to help debugging.
Python Enhancement Proposal: a design document describing a new Python feature or process. PEP 636 is the tutorial for structural pattern matching.
A class-based object-oriented language (1995) running on the JVM, which has added functional features: lambdas and streams (8), records (16), sealed types (17) and pattern matching for switch (21).
A JetBrains language (2011) on the JVM that fuses OOP and functional programming. Classes are final unless marked open.
Microsoft's object-oriented language for .NET (2000), which added functional features such as LINQ and pattern matching.
Language Integrated Query: C# syntax and methods (from C# 3.0, 2007) for querying collections and databases declaratively, like SQL inside the language.
Bjarne Stroustrup's extension of C (1985) with classes, templates and, since C++11, lambdas. C++20 added ranges for pipeline-style code.

A systems language (1.0 in 2015) that is memory-safe without a garbage collector, thanks to ownership rules. It mixes imperative code, traits instead of inheritance, and ML-style enums with pattern matching.
Apple's language (2014) for iOS and macOS apps, pairing classes with value-type structs and enums that carry data.
An object-oriented extension of C with Smalltalk-style messaging, Apple's main language before Swift.
Apple's operating system for the iPhone.
Microsoft's language (2012) that adds static types to JavaScript and compiles to plain JavaScript.
A compact binary instruction format that browsers can run at near-native speed, used as a compilation target for languages such as C, C++ and Rust.
Google's language (2009) for servers and tools. It has no inheritance: it uses struct embedding and interfaces, and has built-in support for concurrency.
Niklaus Wirth's structured, procedural language (1970), widely used for teaching. Its var parameters are passed by reference.
A scripting language (1987) known for text processing. Its local keyword gives a variable a dynamically scoped temporary value.
A dynamic object-oriented scripting language (1995), in which method arguments are passed by sharing.
A small embeddable scripting language (1993) from Brazil, popular in games. Its closures capture variables as upvalues.
The Bourne Again Shell, the standard command language on most Linux systems. Its local variables are dynamically scoped.
The Lisp dialect used to program the Emacs editor. It used dynamic scope by default for decades; lexical scope became available in 2012.
A small Lisp dialect created by Guy Steele and Gerald Sussman in 1975, which showed lexical scope and closures work well in Lisp.
An influential 1960 language that introduced block structure and lexical scope, and passed parameters by name by default.
A language designed by Barbara Liskov's group at MIT (1970s) that pioneered abstract data types and named the 'call by sharing' strategy.
A language for statistics and data analysis. Its function arguments are lazy 'promises', evaluated only when first used.

Philip Wadler's 1998 name for the difficulty of making it easy both to add new data types and to add new operations. OOP makes new types cheap and new operations expensive; pattern matching does the reverse.
American computer scientist, long based in Edinburgh, who helped design Haskell, helped add generics to Java (through the Generic Java project) and named the expression problem in 1998.
A type whose complete list of subtypes is fixed where it is declared, so the compiler can check that a match or switch handles every case. Java has had sealed classes since Java 17.
The compiler confirming that a match or switch handles every possible case of a closed set of variants, and reporting any that are missing. Rust does it; Python's match does not.

A type defined as a fixed set of alternatives, each carrying its own data, such as a Shape that is either a Circle with a radius or a Square with a side. Rust enums and Haskell data types are examples.
A type with a fixed set of named variants. In Rust and Swift each variant can carry data, making enums algebraic data types.
One of the alternatives of an enum or sealed type, such as Circle in a Shape type.
A tree representing a program's structure, with a node for each construct, such as an addition with its two operands as children. Compilers analyse and transform it in passes.
One stage of a compiler that walks the program representation once to check or transform it, such as type checking, constant folding or code generation.
A compiler optimisation that computes expressions with known values at compile time, such as replacing 2 * 3 with 6.
The compiler stage that produces the output program, such as machine code or bytecode, from the internal representation.
A separately written module that adds features to a program through an interface the program defines.
A JavaScript state library in which all state changes go through reducers: pure functions that take the current state and an action and return the new state.
A purely functional language for web front ends (2012) whose architecture has a pure update function that turns the current model and a message into the new model.
Storing every change to a system as an event in an append-only log, and computing the current state by applying the events in order with a pure function.
Wrapping a primitive value such as a Java int in an object such as Integer so it can go where objects are required. It can cost allocation and an extra memory indirection.
An abstraction that compiles to code as fast as writing the low-level version by hand, such as Rust iterator chains compiling to plain loops.
A small computer built into a product, such as a thermostat or car controller, often with tight limits on memory and timing.
Python's core library for fast numerical arrays, the foundation of its data-science ecosystem.
A Python machine-learning library for building and training neural networks.
A Rust trait that controls what the * operator and automatic dereferencing do. Using it to imitate class inheritance is considered an anti-pattern.
A Python function that walks through several iterables one after another without copying them, so flattening n lists takes linear time.
In Rust, a method such as map or filter that wraps an iterator in a new lazy iterator. Chains of them compile to tight loops.
The UK's smallest money unit; 100 pence make a pound. Storing money as a whole number of pence avoids floating-point rounding errors.
Microsoft-owned website for hosting Git code repositories, which also runs the CodeQL analysis engine.
Software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, change and share it.

An order of operations that other code could notice, for example because steps mutate shared state or have side effects. Where there is none, as in pure code, a compiler may reorder or merge the steps freely.
Building programs that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules, such as image classifiers. Python dominates it because of libraries like NumPy and PyTorch.
Extracting knowledge from data with statistics, programming and visualisation.
A call from a function (or Prolog rule) to itself, on a smaller or different input. Each one normally adds a stack frame until it returns.
A sudden, large slowdown when some hidden threshold is crossed, such as a query planner switching to a much worse plan when statistics change.
The order in which a program's expressions and steps are carried out. Imperative code fixes it explicitly; declarative code leaves more of it to the engine.
